stories.headline: Election Commission caps Form 7 applications to prevent bulk voter deletions
stories.title: Election Commission caps Form 7 applications to prevent bulk voter deletions
stories.summary: The new rules require electoral registration officers to verify objections, hear applicants and give affected voters an opportunity to respond before deletion.
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
article_sentences: To prevent bulk or malicious attempts to remove legitimate voters from electoral rolls, the Election Commission on Friday introduced specific caps on how many Form 7 applications a single registered elector can submit.
These restrictions apply equally, whether the forms are submitted online or offline.
During the special period designated for filing claims and objections – typically known as the Summary Revision period – an individual voter is allowed to submit a maximum of 10 Form 7 applications.
Once this revision period concludes, the process shifts to continuous updation.
During this routine period of voter list updation, individual voters are limited to submitting no more than five Form 7 applications in a single calendar month.
Amid reports of bulk filing of such applications or Form 7 from Karnataka and Odisha, the EC has directed all chief electoral officers to brief their field staff about the new directions.
The move aims to discourage bulk filing of unsubstantiated objections, reduce inconvenience to voters and ease the workload of election officials.

According to the reworked mechanism, the electoral registration officer (ERO) will first issue a notice to the objector, hear him personally, record his statements separately for each Form 7 and satisfy himself about the validity of the objections.
When the ERO is satisfied, he will dispose of the application as per Rules 19 and 20 of the Registration of Electors Rules, 1960, giving an opportunity of hearing to the person objected to.
The directive seeks to curb excessive or potentially fabricated objections to electoral rolls while reinforcing verification and procedural safeguards before names are deleted.

The Commission has directed the chief electoral officers of all states and Union Territories to circulate the instructions among the EROs, assistant EROs and field-level officials and ensure adequate publicity.
What is Form 7 and who can file it?

stories.headline: Indian origin jurist Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize
stories.title: Indian origin jurist Navi Pillay wins Nobel Peace Prize
stories.summary: Oslo, Oct 9: South African jurist of Indian origin Navanethem “Navi” Pillay, a former UN human rights chief whose work helped shape international law on genocide and sexual violence, won the 2026 Nobel Peace Prize on Friday for her efforts to promote peace and international law. The 85-year-old jurist, who grew up under apartheid and went on to hold senior positions in South Africa’s judiciary and international legal institutions, dedicated the award to survivors of international crimes and those defending international justice, saying their “compassion and courage continue to ensure that impunity will not be allowed to reign”. “We are living through an era when international law and human rights are under significant political attack,” Pillay said, pointing in particular to attacks on the International Criminal Court (ICC). One of her most recent roles was chairing the UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory. In September 2025, the commission concluded that Israeli authorities and security forces had committed and were continuing to commit genocide against Palestinians in Gaza. The commission also concluded that Israeli President Isaac Herzog, Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and then Defence Minister Yoav Gallant had incited genocide. Israel rejected the findings. The conclusions were those of an investigative body, not a final ruling by an international court. In separate remarks following the Nobel announcement, Pillay referred to the Gaza report as her most recent work, saying it had named what was happening there as genocide. Pillay is also serving as a judge in a case at the International Court of Justice (ICJ) in which The Gambia has accused Myanmar of violating the Genocide Convention. She was selected by The Gambia to sit in the proceedings. Pillay learnt of the Nobel award while attending a forum in Nuremberg, Germany, where Nazi leaders were tried after World War II. She said it was fitting that the announcement came while she was in Courtroom 600, where the trials were held. Warning that efforts to weaken international criminal justice threatened to undo progress made since the Nuremberg trials, the jurist said on Friday: “They risk returning us to a world in which power rather than law determines whose suffering matters.” In a message to political leaders, Pillay said they had a legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war. “My message to leaders, political leaders, is that you are under legal obligation,” she said. “No matter what other obligation you have morally, you have a legal obligation to protect human rights and refrain from war.” She urged countries to uphold the principles of the UN Charter and their obligations under international law, adding: “That is an obligation I call upon every state to fulfill.” Born in Durban on September 23, 1941, to Indian parents of Tamil descent, Pillay grew up in a poor family under apartheid. According to a biographical profile published by the Institute for African Women in Law, her father was a bus driver who worked multiple jobs to support the family, while her mother looked after their eight children. Despite financial hardship, her parents placed a strong emphasis on education and insisted that their daughters, like their sons, should be educated. Pillay studied at the University of Natal, graduating with a Bachelor of Arts degree in 1963 and a law degree in 1965. She later earned postgraduate law degrees at Harvard University, including a doctorate in juridical science in 1988. In 1967, she became the first woman of colour to establish a law practice in South Africa’s Natal Province, according to the Institute for African Women in Law. She spent decades defending anti-apartheid activists and political detainees, including leaders such as Nelson Mandela, and drawing attention to torture and solitary confinement. In 1973, she helped secure political prisoners’ right to legal counsel, according to South African History Online. Her work also exposed the racial barriers within South Africa’s legal system. A Harvard Law School profile noted that, as a lawyer, she had not been allowed to enter a judge’s chambers. Pillay was involved in efforts to enshrine equality in South Africa’s Constitution. As a member of the Women’s National Coalition, she contributed to a campaign that helped secure a constitutional equality clause prohibiting discrimination. In an interview with South African History Online, she described how women from different political, racial and religious backgrounds worked together to advance equality and protect women’s rights. In 1995, a year after South Africa’s first democratic elections, Pillay became the first woman of colour to serve as an acting judge on the country’s High Court. That same year, she was elected to the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda, established to prosecute those responsible for genocide and other serious crimes committed during the 1994 genocide in Rwanda. She served as a judge until 2003 and was the tribunal’s president from 1999 to 2003. One of the most consequential chapters of her judicial career was her work as one of the judges in the tribunal’s landmark case against Jean-Paul Akayesu, the former mayor of Taba commune, who was convicted of genocide, crimes against humanity and direct and public incitement to commit genocide. The tribunal’s 1998 judgment recognised that rape and sexual violence could constitute acts of genocide when committed with the specific intent required under the Genocide Convention. It also recognised rape as a crime against humanity in the circumstances established in the case. Akayesu’s conviction for direct and public incitement to commit genocide also established an important precedent in international criminal law. The Norwegian Nobel Committee credited Pillay with playing a significant role in the legal development concerning sexual violence. Speaking after the Nobel announcement, Pillay said she was proud that the tribunal had recognised sexual violence as an international crime. She described it as “outrageous” that sexual violence against women and children in conflict had been treated as “collateral damage or as reward for the hard fighting soldiers”. Pillay subsequently served as a judge at the International Criminal Court from 2003 to 2008, including on its Appeals Chamber, and as the UN High Commissioner for Human Rights from 2008 to 2014. She also co-founded Equality Now in 1992 alongside Jessica Neuwirth and Feryal Gharahi. The international women’s rights organisation works to advance women’s rights and challenge discriminatory laws and practices. The Norwegian Nobel Committee said the award recognised Pillay’s efforts to promote peace and international law, highlighting her role in ensuring that war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted. The committee described her as “a person who, with exceptional courage and integrity, has led the way towards a more comprehensive legal order”. It said she had been instrumental in ensuring that “war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide are prosecuted”. It also praised her commitment to universal legal principles and said she had helped hold states and national leaders accountable while bringing hope to victims of violence and conflict. “Peace requires justice,” the committee said, arguing that a legal system in which war criminals are held accountable and victims of abuse see justice served is a precondition for a peaceful world. South African President Cyril Ramaphosa congratulated Pillay on behalf of the nation, describing the award as a tribute to her courage, integrity and lifelong commitment to justice. “Justice Pillay’s crowning as winner of the Nobel Prize allows us to celebrate the progressive contributions she has made to strengthen peace, uphold human dignity and bring hope in South Africa and to peoples globally,” Ramaphosa said in a statement issued by his office. He said she had “served humanity with principle and the belief that the world can and should be a better place”. European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen also congratulated Pillay, praising her lifelong commitment to justice, peace and human dignity in a post on X. “Few have devoted their lives to justice, peace and human dignity like she did,” von der Leyen said. “From the violence of apartheid in South Africa to the horrors of the Rwandan genocide, she has confronted some of humanity’s darkest chapters. She has looked the brutality of injustice in the eye and never looked away.” The Nobel Peace Prize was first awarded in 1901. The 2026 award marks its 125th anniversary.

stories.headline: Wars and unintended consequences
stories.title: Wars and unintended consequences
stories.summary: A week after the US and Iran launched the Iran war I wrote in these columns, on March 6, that all wars were likely not to proceed as expected by those who began them; that they were subject to the law of unintended consequences. The Iran war has proved to be no exception. Reports indicate the Israeli intelligence persuaded a willing Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu that a decapitating strike would lead to the extinction of Iran’s vilayat-e-faqih system through a popular uprising. It is likely that they pointed to the January riots in Iran which were fuelled by great economic distress. It would appear that Netanyahu was able to bring US President Donald Trump to the same conclusion. Trump was greatly buoyed up by the quick success achieved by US forces in capturing Venezuela’s President Nicolas Maduro and his wife from Caracas this January. There have also been credible news reports that some sections of his administration, including a few of his senior colleagues, had advised Trump against beginning the Iran war. However, Trump had the bit between his teeth and went ahead. He is now facing unanticipated problems. The law of unintended consequences has caught up with him. This has been vividly brought out by one of the leading newspapers of not only the US but the world. Trump calls its reports as fake news but the newspaper is respected the world over and its credibility is high even if its ideological disposition is far removed from Trump’s maverick conservatism. In a long report a few days ago the newspaper revealed the following points: • that during the ongoing Iran war US forces have “been forced into retreat, pulling back military forces that had been deployed to the Middle East and Britain as a deterrent”. (These are not tactical retreats because of optimising forces for use in the war but out of fear that Iran will find new ways of damaging US forces at their present locations) • “the Iran war has come to reveal enormous new American vulnerabilities, forcing changes that the Pentagon was not contemplating a year ago…rather than enhance American power, the war has constrained it”. • the war has “vastly complicated the logistics of projecting power. American bombers”. • “...most importantly, the rapid withdrawals have taught a lesson to the Iranians — and potentially to other adversaries — that they hold the power to chase out a superpower”. • “...keeping forces out of missile range is not enough. Drones and cyberweapons have reshaped the battlefield”. • though the US has destroyed Iran’s navy and airforce, “keeping [US] forces out of missile range is not enough. Drones and cyberweapons have reshaped the battlefield”. • Iran has forced “American aircraft and personnel to flee their once-secure bases farther and farther from Iran. American personnel were evacuated from bases in Bahrain, Kuwait, the United Arab Emirates and Qatar, all of which were within Iranian missile and drone range. Some of those bases were so badly damaged that inside the Pentagon there is little interest in rebuilding them; they will be moved farther away, if Congress grants the funding”. • the US “has been unable to guarantee “freedom of navigation” through the Strait of Hormuz or parts of the Red Sea”. • “This was not the plan when Mr. Trump announced the attack on Iran on Feb. 28. Mr. Trump was looking for a victory in a few days, then five or six weeks. Mr. Trump demanded “unconditional surrender,” and three weeks into the conflict declared Iran’s total defeat. Last Thursday, he said Iran would fold “right after the election”. Taken together this news report constitutes a devastating account of how the war has gone for the US and Israel. More importantly it will impact the methods of war fighting especially when a mighty military power attacks a state without the wherewithal to combat it through conventional forces. That will naturally only be if the state so attacked is willing to endure enormous economic hardships but its people show a national spirit not to let the attacking state have its way. In Venezuela the ruling apparatus simply and quickly folded up after a single raid which captured its President and his wife and took them to the US to be tried as criminals in a US court. On the other hand in Iran despite a decapitating strike the ruling establishment endured and found new and novel ways of striking back. This is reminiscent of the Vietnam war where the Vietcong withstood years of a US war but eventually forced it out. That the Iran war has already begun to lead to geo-political and geo-strategic changes in West Asia is clear. The Saudi-Turkey-Pact and Netanyahu’s short visit to the UAE on September 27 are harbingers of this change. The fractures in the Arab Gulf states had occurred before the Iran war but these manifestations are more meaningful than what was on the surface earlier. What will be the final shape of the region will take time to emerge only after the war ends. That will impact on the region’s interests, including India’s in strategic, economic and commercial and the energy fields among others. That the US will remain the world’s pre-eminent power any which way the Iran war ends is not in doubt. What is in question is how the world will perceive it in relation to the rising power, China, which is close on its heels? Many states particularly in the Indo-Pacific region have already begun to hedge between the two of them. In these circumstances how will India play the game of nations?

stories.headline: Mediation must be preferred choice, not last resort: J&K HC judge
stories.title: Mediation must be preferred choice, not last resort: J&K HC judge
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 9: Mediation should be the preferred choice for dispute resolution rather than a last resort, Justice Rajnesh Oswal, Chairman of the Mediation and Conciliation Committee of the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, said as a 40-hour role-play training programme for advocates and experts concluded at the J&K Judicial Academy campuses in Srinagar and Jammu on Friday. Justice Oswal encouraged participants to apply their newly acquired skills in practice and contribute to the Mediation for the Nation 3.0 initiative, emphasising the role of mediation in facilitating amicable settlements and helping parties move forward without bitterness. He said the spirit of mediation was inherent in everyday life, from families and schools to communities and professional relationships. Drawing on his judicial experience, he explained how mediation could help resolve even long-pending disputes where a settlement initially appeared unlikely. The training programme was organised under the aegis of the Mediation and Conciliation Project Committee (MCPC) of the Supreme Court of India by the Mediation and Conciliation Committee of the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, in collaboration with the J&K Judicial Academy. The practical sessions were held on October 5, 6, 8 and 9. During the second day of the Srinagar session, Chief Justice of the High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh, Dr Justice Pushpendra Singh Bhati, highlighted the importance of mediation in strengthening the justice delivery system. He said mediation was not merely a professional skill but also a means of becoming a better human being and a more effective advocate, public prosecutor or judge. He emphasised that practical exercises and role-play sessions helped develop empathy, understanding and sensitivity in resolving disputes. Referring to Indian epics, religious traditions and Kashmir's history, the Chief Justice highlighted the longstanding cultural significance of peaceful dispute resolution. He also referred to Surah An-Nisa of the Holy Quran, observing that its provisions envisage a process resembling modern mediation, with representatives from both sides appointed to help restore harmony. Justice Bhati said examples across religious and cultural traditions demonstrated the enduring relevance of reconciliation and amicable settlement. Rajeev Gupta, in-charge Director of the J&K Judicial Academy, welcomed the dignitaries, resource persons and participants, stressing the importance of practical training in developing effective mediation skills. stories.headline: Kashmir slipping into darkness!
stories.title: Kashmir slipping into darkness!
stories.summary: Jammu and Kashmir is known as the “Paradise on Earth” by virtue of its astonishing natural landscapes, snow-capped mountains, crystal-clear lakes, and vibrant changing seasons. The region is endowed with massive mountain ranges like the Himalayas and Pir Panjal, deep green valleys, meadows, and pristine water bodies & rivers like Dal Lake, Wular, and Jhelum. Spring brings blooming tulip gardens, yellow mustard fields and pink almond flowers around karewas of Pulwama and Budgam. The summer offers lush greenery, gushing waters in streams , the autumn turns the trees into vibrant gold and red hues, and winter turns the region into a snowy wonderland. Sadly the current situation - “surat e haal” - does not offer a rosy picture of Kashmir. As per the recent National Clean Air Survey (Swachh Vayu Survekshan) Srinagar has been ranked at 26th place among 39 Indian cities with a population of 10 lakh or more. In the first survey that was launched in 2023 Srinagar ranked 4th. What has happened in last 3 years that Srinagar came down 22 steps downwards ? Burning of MSW The municipal solid waste is being burnt openly by sanitation staff across J&K and even Srinagar. Dust control mechanism is not in place. There has been a mushroom growth of vehicles emitting vehicular emission and causing heavy damage to ambient air quality. Illegal cement plants and stone crushers have are running openly without appropriate checks. No suitable measures have been taken for construction and demolition waste management system. There is lack of public awareness regarding air pollution by authorities and all these things contribute for air pollution in Srinagar and other districts of J&K. Last year the Air Quality Index -AQI touched almost 300 and this autumn and early winter would be terrible. Govt has to act and MLAs must put pressure on authorities during the ongoing session of assembly ? It is a matter of concern that Srinagar is behind Delhi vis a vis air quality. Delhi has for long made headlines with toxic winter smog and features among India’s most persistent air-pollution. Delhi secured the 21st rank with 172 points and Srinagar scored 162.6 points with 26th rank. According to the survey Lucknow ranks number one followed by Indore, Jabalpur, and Bhopal. The Swachh Vayu Survekshan Clean Air Survey was initiated in 2023 by the Government of India Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEFCC) under its National Clean Air Programme-NCAP and the survey is conducted by the Central Pollution Control Board-CPCB New Delhi. Although more than half of 130 non-attainment cities spent less than 50 per cent of the funds released under NCAP and 15th Finance Commission grants, Jammu and Kashmir offers a unsettling scene regarding utilisation of funds received under NCAP. Jammu & Kashmir received Rs 21 Crores between 2019 to June 2022 under NCPA crore but only Rs 12 lakh was spent constituting merely 0.5 per cent ? If less than 1 % of the funds were spent over three years soon since NCAP was launched, programme execution and implementation raises questions regarding accountability. When we compare this with states like Gujarat, Andhra Pradesh or Himachal they have spent good amount of money. In the same period Gujarat got Rs 12 crore and spent 100 per cent of the funds. Andhra Pradesh received Rs 34 crore and spent Rs 22 crore, while Himachal Pradesh received Rs 10 crore and spent Rs 6.30 crore as per the information provided by Ministry of Environment Forest and Climate Change. CAG Report As far as environmental degradation vis a vis waterbodies and lakes of Jammu & Kashmir are concerned, the story is not different. The recent CAG report has disclosed that more than 500 lakes in Jammu and Kashmir have either vanished or significantly receded due to encroachments, siltation, and untreated sewage inflow, weakening natural flood buffers. Of the total lakes, 315 (45 %) covering 1,537.07 hectares have completely disappeared from official records. These include 80 lakes under the jurisdiction of the Forest / Wildlife Department and 235 under the Revenue and Agriculture departments. The report warned that the disappearance and shrinkage of 518 lakes have led to ecosystem degradation, loss of water resources, food and biodiversity, and disruption of carbon, nutrient, and water cycles, heightening climate vulnerability in the region. The primary reasons for the disappearance and shrinkage of lakes were identified as land-use changes within lakes and their catchment areas. Other contributing factors include deforestation, climate change, and altered catchment dynamics. The CAG audit also underlined deficiencies in conservation and management practices. According to the report, government conservation efforts were limited to only six lakes—Dal, Wular, Hokersar, Manasbal, Surinsar, and Mansar—which were examined in detail. For the remaining 691 lakes, the Forest Department neither identified eligible water bodies nor formulated plans to seek assistance under schemes of the Ministry of Environment, Forest and Climate Change (MoEF&CC). The audit also flagged several issues affecting Dal Lake, including land-use changes due to non-acquisition of land from dwellers, malfunctioning sewage treatment plants (STPs), ineffective de-weeding mechanisms, and inadequate monitoring and surveillance. The CAG has recommended the establishment of a centralised and specialised authority equipped with adequate resources to ensure coordinated, accountable, and effective lake conservation and management. It also called for the deployment of skilled manpower, including environmental and hydrological engineers, wetland ecologists, limnologists, remote sensing and GIS specialists. SC, NGT intervention Fresh cloudbursts in the Pir Panjal & Chenab Valley, the rapid melting of the Amarnath ice lingam, mountains of untreated waste and relentless riverbed mining are jaw-dropper crises. Even Supreme Court has expressed concern over illegal mining in Shaliganga stream in the case of Govt of J&K & others v/s Raja Muzaffar Bhat Civil Appeal No. 8055 of 2022. After the Apex Courts Judgement dated August 22nd 2025 the J&K Pollution Control Committee -JKPCC has imposed Environmental Compensation of Rs 3.10 crore on a construction company NKC Projects Pvt Ltd in Feb 2026. This amount had to be paid in 3 months and now with the lapse of 6 months , the penalty amount has surged 3 times. The company has to pay Rs 12.30 crore and JKPCC has now asked the National Highway Authority of India -NHAI to retrieve the compensation money from pending bills of the company. This information was revealed on the floor of J&K Assembly few days back by J&K’s Mining Minister in response to MLA of Chadoora assembly segment in Budgam district. The last year’s cloudburst in Chisoti village in Kishtwar district claiming more than 75 people is still fresh in the minds of the people of Jammu and Kashmir. Another cloudburst had now struck the region, triggering flash floods and mudslides that damaged roads in Doda, Kishtwar and Ramban. Transport along the Jammu-Doda-Kishtwar highway came to a halt. Illegal mining of sand, gravel and boulders has intensified in recent years, damaging streams from Kathua to Kupwara and Budgam to Baramulla. In addition to it illegal earth mining in the Karewas of Budgam , Pulwama, Baramulla , Anantnag has caused devastation in these areas and NGT has taken cognizance of this case as well. The JKPCCs report submitted in NGT few months back revealed that 18 lakh Metric Tons clay, sand and gravel were excavated from just two villages of Gowherpora and Zadoora alone in Budgam and Pulwama districts. Although legal action through the National Green Tribunal has curbed machine-based extraction in rivers such as Doodh Ganga, Shaliganga and Sukhnag, manual extraction continues and cumulative damage has transformed river channels. Conclusion Jammu and Kashmir has reached the point where piecemeal responses no longer match the scale of the challenge. Climate adaptation must guide infrastructure planning, pilgrimage management, mining enforcement, waste processing, groundwater protection and disaster preparedness through one coordinated strategy backed by measurable goals and public accountability. Government declarations alone solve little. Public recognition changes priorities, mobilizes resources and signals that environmental protection sits alongside economic development instead of behind it. Jammu and Kashmir now faces a choice between continued crisis management and a comprehensive climate response. K P Yadaw is former Principal Accountant General J&K who was posted in J&K just before his retirement in Oct 2025 Raja Muzaffar Bhat is Founder of J&K RTI Movement , Chairman of J&K Climate Action Group

stories.headline: ECI’s credibility damaged, Gyanesh Kumar must resign: National Conference
stories.title: ECI’s credibility damaged, Gyanesh Kumar must resign: National Conference
stories.summary: Srinagar, Oct 9: The Jammu and Kashmir National Conference Friday strongly condemned the reported detentions of young people across the country ahead of INDIA block, CJP protest in Delhi against the Election Commission of India in New Delhi, police announcements in mosques asking people not to participate in the protest, cancellation of train services and measures to turn the national capital into a security forces cantonment. The party, as per a statement issued, described these actions as contrary to democratic principles and the Constitution. The party's Additional General Secretary and Rajya Sabha MP Chowdry Mohammad Ramzan said that the reality behind the BJP's repeated electoral victories had now come to light before the people of the country. He said that 9.7 million voters were excluded from the electoral rolls in West Bengal ahead of the elections, which contributed to the defeat of Mamata Banerjee's party, despite pre-election surveys and analyses indicating a likely victory for the Trinamool Congress. Chowdry Mohammad Ramzan said that the Election Commission had removed the names of 170 million voters across the country over the past several years, representing approximately 15 percent of the country's population. He said the Commission was duty-bound to ensure that every eligible citizen who had attained the age of 18 was registered as a voter. However the Commission was acting contrary to this responsibility by deleting people's names from the electoral rolls, a development he described as deeply unfortunate, alarming and a serious blow to democracy. He said recent revelations concerning the Election Commission of India had raised serious questions about the institution's credibility and that the matter was now also under consideration before the Supreme Court. Referring to the Supreme Court's observations, Chowdry Mohammad Ramzan said the Court had stated that it had no information regarding the permission for Form 6. He termed the matter serious, adding that falsely invoking the Supreme Court's permission to benefit a particular political party was an issue of grave concern. He said the circumstances demanded that the Chief Election Commissioner resign from office, arguing that the credibility of an institution entrusted with safeguarding the sanctity of democracy had been severely undermined. Chowdry Mohammad Ramzan strongly condemned the reported detentions across the country aimed at thwarting the protest scheduled by the CJP in New Delhi on October 10. He also criticised the alleged intimidation of Muslims to prevent them from participating in the protest, the suspension of railway services, the closure of metro stations and measures to turn the national capital into a military cantonment. He said the Constitution of India guaranteed every citizen the right to peaceful protest. However those in power were resorting to unconstitutional and undemocratic methods in an attempt to conceal their wrongdoings. Chowdry Mohammad Ramzan also strongly condemned the police restrictions imposed in recent days on protests by opposition Members of Parliament and prominent leaders. He said that if elected representatives of the people were being subjected to such treatment, the plight of ordinary citizens could only be imagined.

stories.headline: Supreme Court Orders Regulated Metro Services Amid CJP Protest Plans in Delhi
stories.title: Supreme Court Orders Regulated Metro Services Amid CJP Protest Plans in Delhi
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: New Delhi: The Supreme Court on Friday ordered that there should be no complete stoppage of Metro train services ahead of the proposed protest in the national capital on Saturday, and directed the Centre to ensure that Metro and other railway services are allowed to operate in a suitably regulated manner to minimise inconvenience to the public.
Even as the CJP is bent on going ahead with the shutdown, the Delhi.
Police today said permission for the demonstration has been denied due to the organisers' failure to comply with legal directions and their own undertakings during an earlier protest.

A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana passed the order after Solicitor General Tushar Mehta agreed to impress upon the authorities to reconsider the restrictions imposed ahead of a proposed demonstration by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) seeking accountability from Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The apex court said the issue before it was whether the complete stoppage of Metro trains and railway services from certain stations constituted a proportionate restriction in view of the proposed protest.

Observing that there was a distinction between completely prohibiting movement and regulating services, the CJI-led Bench said the authorities should keep the principle of proportionality in mind while taking preventive measures.

SG Mehta, the Centre's second-highest law officer, assured the top court that the authorities would reconsider the prohibition and allow the movement of Metro trains and other railway services in a regulated manner so that residents of Delhi and the public at large did not face inconvenience.
"In terms of that assurance, we make it clear that there shall be no complete prohibition on the movement of metro trains," the Supreme Court said.

It also directed the authorities to give wide publicity to their considered decision on the regulated operation of Metro and other railway services so that commuters were not subjected to further inconvenience.
It further directed that a traffic advisory be published for the benefit of people travelling within the national capital to ensure that they did not face unnecessary hardship.
The CJI-led Bench asked the Centre to consider the proposal and take an appropriate decision on designating a suitable venue for such demonstrations.

The order came amid concerns over the proposed closure of 57 Metro stations and the cancellation or rescheduling of several trains scheduled to arrive at New Delhi and Hazrat Nizamuddin railway stations on October 10.

It further directed that a traffic advisory be published for the benefit of people travelling within the national capital to ensure that they did not face unnecessary hardship.

sentences.text: New Delhi: The Supreme Court on Friday ordered that there should be no complete stoppage of Metro train services ahead of the proposed protest in the national capital on Saturday, and directed the Centre to ensure that Metro and other railway services are allowed to operate in a suitably regulated manner to minimise inconvenience to the public.
Police today said permission for the demonstration has been denied due to the organisers' failure to comply with legal directions and their own undertakings during an earlier protest.

A Bench of Chief Justice of India (CJI) Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V. Mohana passed the order after Solicitor General Tushar Mehta agreed to impress upon the authorities to reconsider the restrictions imposed ahead of a proposed demonstration by the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) seeking accountability from Chief Election Commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.
